statement: In published cases of cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (bouts of severe nausea and vomiting, again and again, in people who use cannabis regularly), pooled descriptively in a systematic review of reports from 2000 to September 2015 (Sorensen et al., 2017; AMSTAR 2 critically low; 211 patients from 80 case reports and 7 case series, 98 of them from one series entered as summary figures; no randomized trials, no comparison groups and no count of how many people who use cannabis develop the syndrome), all patients had recurrent vomiting with severe nausea and 85.1% had abdominal pain; 154 of 211 (72.9%) were men; the median age was 16 at first cannabis use (IQR 14 to 18; 84 patients), 24 at the start of symptoms (19 to 29; 101) and 28 at diagnosis (22 to 34; 111). Of the 197 whose frequency of use was reported, 76.6% used cannabis daily or more often and 97.4% at least weekly, and 45 of 179 (25.1%) had used for a year or less before symptoms began. Of the patients whose bathing was reported, 157 of 170 (92.3%) found that hot baths or showers relieved their symptoms. Of the 64 patients whose stopping was documented, 62 (96.8%) had complete resolution of symptoms; the two without resolution had no urine test to confirm that they had stopped, and all 21 patients who kept using still had symptoms. Follow-up was documented for only 85 of the 211 patients (40.2%), no time to resolution is reported, and whether symptoms returned when people started again was too inconsistently documented to count. The review proposes recognising the syndrome by severe cyclic vomiting, usually with abdominal pain, at least weekly cannabis use before symptoms began, temporary relief with hot bathing and resolution after stopping, with male sex, starting cannabis in the teenage years and symptoms beginning in the twenties as supporting features; these features come from cases diagnosed by them, so their frequencies do not show how well they separate the syndrome from other causes of repeated vomiting, which no study in the review tested. Diagnosis came on average 4.1 years (SD 4.6) after symptoms began, and in four case reports patients were first diagnosed with severe vomiting of pregnancy. A 2021 review says the distinction from other cyclic vomiting disorders is underdeveloped and cites two sources for 90% of patients reporting that hot baths and stopping cannabis relieve their symptoms (Connor et al., 2021; second-hand), and a 2014 review links repeated use with increased vomiting without a citation (Volkow et al., 2014). All nine proposed mechanisms were rated very low, and three cases involved synthetic cannabinoids; acute hospital treatments are covered in the claims on capsaicin cream and on dopamine-blocking medicines. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Cannabis hyperemesis syndrome means bouts of severe nausea and vomiting, usually with belly pain, in people who use cannabis regularly. In 211 published cases, about three in four used cannabis daily or more, but a quarter had used it for a year or less before the bouts began, and most found that hot baths or showers eased the symptoms for a while. Of the 64 cases where stopping was recorded, 62 got completely better, and the 21 people who kept using did not. These are published cases only: nobody knows from them how common the syndrome is, fewer than half of the cases had any follow-up written down, and the signs used to recognise it come from the same cases, so how well they tell it apart from other vomiting illnesses has not been tested. On average it took about 4 years from the first symptoms to the diagnosis.
population: Patients with a clinician's diagnosis of cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome described in published case reports and case series, 2000 to 2015 (211 patients; 72.9% men; median age at diagnosis 28)
exposure: Regular cannabis use as reported in each case (frequency known for 197, duration for 179); three cases involved synthetic cannabinoids
comparator: None (case descriptions); for resolution, patients who stopped compared with those who kept using
outcome: Features of the syndrome as recorded; relief with hot bathing; resolution of symptoms after stopping cannabis
magnitude: Sorensen 2017 cumulative synthesis (211 patients; each share is of the patients in whom the feature was reported): recurrent vomiting 100% (211); severe nausea and vomiting 100% (211); abdominal pain 85.1% (202); relief with hot bathing 92.3% (157 of 170); resolution after stopping 96.8% (62 of 64; all 21 who kept using had ongoing symptoms); at least weekly use 97.4% (197); daily or more 76.6% (197); regular use for more than a year 74.8% (179); men 72.9% (154 of 211). Duration of use before onset (179): 1 year or less 25.1%, 2-5 years 36.3%, 6-10 years 16.8%, 11 years or more 21.8%. Median ages: first use 16 (IQR 14-18; 84), onset 24 (19-29; 101), diagnosis 28 (22-34; 111). Mean delay to diagnosis 4.1 years (SD 4.6). Follow-up documented for 85 of 211 (40.2%).

risk_of_bias.note: Published case reports and series chosen by clinicians who decided to report them, often cases resembling the first description; the features counted are those used to make the diagnosis; outcomes documented for a minority (stopping for 64, any follow-up for 85 of 211) and abstinence not verified; no risk-of-bias tool applied by the review (card sc_sorensen_2017, AMSTAR 2 critically low).

inconsistency.note: The case reports and series describe the same features; some series' numbers differ between the review's text and tables (card reporting issues), which does not change the picture.

indirectness.note: Published, mostly hospital-diagnosed cases cannot stand for everyone who develops the syndrome, and the case features answer how it is recognised only as descriptions, not as tested diagnostic criteria.

imprecision.note: Not downgraded separately; the floor is reached.

publication_bias.note: Selection into publication is counted under risk of bias.

grade.reasoning: Case reports and series are observational and start low; down two levels for risk of bias (selection, circular diagnosis, incomplete follow-up) and one for indirectness: very low, the floor. Status replicated: the same picture (recurrent vomiting with regular use, relief with hot water, resolution after stopping) comes from many case reports and several series by different teams, though they reach the claim through one review and the series inside it are not counted again (card sc_sorensen_2017). Connor et al. (2021) cite one of those series (98 patients), so their 90% is not separate evidence. The resolution figure describes documented cases, not what happens to everyone who stops.

statement: As summarised in a 2007 narrative review of controlled-administration studies, most of them small, in men who had used cannabis before, with single doses of low-THC cigarettes or of oral THC, and many from the author's own laboratory (Huestis, 2007; figures second-hand; no systematic search), smoking cannabis is associated with THC reaching the blood within minutes, eating it with slower, lower and later blood levels, and frequent use with THC staying in the body for days to weeks. Smoked: in 6 men who each smoked one cigarette of 1.75% or 3.55% THC (about 16 or 34 mg; study conditions), THC appeared in plasma with the first puff, peaked at a mean of 84.3 and 162.2 ng/ml at 9.0 minutes, fell to about 60% and 20% of the peak 15 and 30 minutes after smoking, and was 5 ng/ml or less within 2 hours, staying detectable (at 0.5 ng/ml) for 3 to 12 hours after the lower and 6 to 27 hours after the higher dose; the strongest effects came later, 30 to 45 minutes after smoking began, when blood levels were already falling. How much of the THC in a cigarette reached the blood varied with how people smoked, from 2% to 56% across studies (about 8% to 24% in others). Eaten: THC was absorbed more slowly, with lower, later and more irregular peaks; after 20 mg of THC in a chocolate cookie, plasma peaks of 4.4 to 11 ng/ml came 1 to 5 hours after eating, with about 6% of the dose reaching the blood, and a study using a radiolabel method, which the author says overestimated THC, found peaks about 4 to 6 hours after 15 to 20 mg in oil; the review puts oral bioavailability at 4% to 20%, because THC is partly broken down in the stomach and much of it is converted in the liver, among other products into 11-OH-THC, which is active and reaches levels similar to or higher than those of THC after eating, against about a tenth of THC after smoking. Compared with smoking, effects after eating began later and lasted longer. THC is almost entirely bound to lipoproteins in the blood (95% to 99%) and is stored in body fat; in people who use frequently, its final plasma half-life was about 4.1 days in a study with long sampling (24 to 36 hours in studies with shorter sampling), and THC-COOH, the breakdown product that urine tests measure, had a plasma half-life of up to 12.6 days in one person. Blood: in people who use frequently, low levels remain between uses (THC 0.86 ng/ml on average at least 12 hours after last use in one study), and a very sensitive method detected a labelled dose of THC for up to 13 days in people who used chronically. Urine: after one smoked cigarette, urine tested positive for THC-COOH at a cut-off of 15 ng/ml for an average of 33.7 hours (8 to 68.5) after the 1.75% and 88.6 hours (57 to 122.3) after the 3.55% cigarette, with positive and negative samples alternating near the cut-off; in two people with heavy use, urine stayed positive for up to 67 days (one person, at 20 ng/ml, after more than 10 years of heavy use) and 93 days. A positive urine test shows that a person was exposed, not when, how much, by which route or whether they were impaired. These studies predate today's stronger products, edibles, vaporizers and concentrates, mostly involved men and gave fixed doses, so they do not show what happens when people who feel little at first take more. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: In small lab studies from before 2007, mostly of men smoking weak cannabis cigarettes, THC in the blood was highest within minutes of smoking (at about 9 minutes) and fell to low levels within 2 hours, while the felt effects were strongest a little later, at 30 to 45 minutes. When THC was eaten, it entered the blood slowly and at lower levels, peaking 1 to 6 hours later, and the effects began later and lasted longer. THC is stored in body fat and, in people who use often, leaves the body over days to weeks. After one cigarette, urine tests stayed positive for about 1 to 4 days on average; in two people who used heavily, for up to 67 and 93 days. A positive test shows use, not when, how much or whether someone was impaired. The studies gave set doses, so they do not show what happens when people who feel little at first take more.
population: Mostly men who had used cannabis before, in small controlled-administration studies summarised by a 2007 narrative review (6 men in the main smoking and urine studies; 17 volunteers in a capsule study), and single case reports of heavy long-term use
exposure: A single smoked cigarette of 1.75% or 3.55% THC (about 16 or 34 mg) or oral THC (20 mg in a cookie; 15 to 20 mg in oil; a 10 mg dronabinol capsule), given by researchers (study conditions only); frequent or heavy long-term use for elimination and detection windows
comparator: Smoking compared with eating; frequent compared with occasional use
outcome: Plasma THC, 11-OH-THC and THC-COOH over time; bioavailability; elimination half-lives; detection windows in plasma and urine
magnitude: Smoked (6 men): mean plasma THC peaks 84.3 ng/ml (range 50-129) and 162.2 ng/ml (76-267) at 9.0 minutes; about 60% and 20% of peak at 15 and 30 minutes; 5 ng/ml or less within 2 hours; detectable at 0.5 ng/ml for 3-12 and 6-27 hours; peak effects 30-45 minutes after smoking began; bioavailability 2%-56% (or about 8%-24%). Oral: 20 mg in a cookie, peaks 4.4-11 ng/ml at 1-5 hours, bioavailability about 6%; 15-20 mg in oil, peaks at about 4-6 hours (radiolabel); 10 mg dronabinol (17 volunteers), THC 3.8 ng/ml (1.1-12.7), 11-OH-THC 3.4 (1.2-5.6), THC-COOH 26 (14-46) at 1-2 hours; summary bioavailability 4%-20%; 11-OH-THC about 10% of THC after smoking, similar or higher after eating. Elimination: terminal plasma THC half-life about 4.1 days with frequent use (24-36 hours with shorter sampling); THC-COOH plasma half-life up to 12.6 days in one person; frequent use, plasma THC 0.86 ng/ml at least 12 hours after last use; deuterated THC detectable up to 13 days (limit 0.02 ng/ml). Urine (6 men, 15 ng/ml cut-off): last positive 33.7 hours (8-68.5) and 88.6 hours (57-122.3) after one cigarette; heavy use, up to 67 days (20 ng/ml) and 93 days in two individuals.

risk_of_bias.note: The primary studies cannot be appraised from the review, which describes no designs or appraisal; much of the human data come from the author's laboratory, some from conference presentations; early radiolabel methods overestimated THC (card sc_huestis_2007, editors' checklist overall high).

inconsistency.note: The contrast between smoking and eating is consistent across the studies described; the spread of smoked bioavailability (2% to 56%) reflects how people smoked and is reported, not pooled.

indirectness.note: Second-hand (METHODS §6.3), and the products and people differ from today's: low-THC cigarettes and single doses, mostly men who had used before, little on daily use, nothing on vaporizers, concentrates or commercial edibles.

imprecision.note: Tiny samples (6 men in the main smoking and urine studies) with large differences between people; the weeks-long urine windows rest on single cases.

grade.reasoning: The cited human studies gave known doses under controlled conditions, and such evidence starts high (as for the methamphetamine pharmacokinetic claims); seen only through a narrative review, it is rated down one level each for risk of bias (not appraisable, much from one laboratory), indirectness (second-hand, old products) and imprecision: very low. Starting low instead, because the review does not describe how the studies were designed, gives the same result. The claim rests only on a narrative review, so it stays at draft and says its figures are second-hand (METHODS §6.3). Status replicated: the review describes the same contrast between smoking and eating from several groups (for example Ohlsson et al., 1980; Wall et al., 1983; Huestis et al., 1992), although the urine detection windows come from single studies and cases.

statement: In observational samples of people who used cannabis regularly or had a cannabis use disorder, the share with cannabis withdrawal, as each study defined it, depended strongly on where the sample came from, in a 2020 meta-analysis of 50 cohorts with 23,518 participants (searched to June 2019; Bahji et al., 2020; AMSTAR 2 critically low; English only; no group of people who did not cut down for comparison): 17 in 100 (95% CI 13 to 22) in 15 general-population samples holding 17,475 people, 54 in 100 (48 to 59) in 28 outpatient samples (5,684 people) and 87 in 100 (79 to 94) in 7 inpatient or residential samples (357 people). Withdrawal at any time in life was reported far more often than withdrawal in the past year (76 in 100, 70 to 82, in 18 cohorts, against 31 in 100, 27 to 36, in 32), and the one general-population sample assessed with DSM-5 criteria found it in 12.1% of 1,527 people. The review's headline figure, 47 in 100 (41 to 52; I2 99.2%; cohorts from 8% to 100%), is close to the plain average of the cohort estimates and is driven by small clinical samples; the review's own count, 6,469 of 23,518 participants, is about 27.5 in 100 (editors' calculation on the study card). Men and women did not differ (27 and 26 in 100, 15 studies), although the review's conclusions say withdrawal was more common in men. In DSM-5, cannabis withdrawal means at least three of seven symptoms within about a week of stopping or cutting down: irritability, anger or aggression; nervousness or anxiety; sleep difficulty; less appetite or weight loss; restlessness; low mood; and physical symptoms such as headache, sweating or stomach pain (as summarised by Bahji et al., 2020, and Connor et al., 2021). As described in narrative reviews, whose figures are second-hand, symptoms typically begin 1 to 2 days after stopping, peak within the first week (at 2 to 6 days in one account) and fade within 1 to 2 weeks (Curran et al., 2016; Connor et al., 2021); craving, nightmares and nausea are also prominent, and THC relieves the symptoms in a dose-dependent way (Curran et al., 2016); people seeking help to stop most often report anxiety, sleep problems, appetite disturbance and low mood (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009), often severe enough to impair everyday life (Hall, 2015); one review gives around half of people who use daily as having withdrawal when they stop, citing an earlier review (Curran et al., 2016); and in people without other medical or psychiatric illness withdrawal is described as carrying no serious risk and usually needing only supportive care (Connor et al., 2021). Sleep after stopping is covered in more detail in the claims on sleep. The cohorts defined regular use differently, most predate DSM-5, the review took the lowest threshold where studies offered several, cohorts with more tobacco use reported more withdrawal (a comparison between studies), and in people who use both daily, stopping both gives stronger symptoms than stopping either alone (Curran et al., 2016). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: When people who use cannabis regularly stop or cut down, some get withdrawal: irritability or anger, nervousness, poor sleep, less appetite, restlessness, low mood, or physical symptoms such as headaches. A 2020 review found it in about 17 in 100 people with regular use in general-population surveys, 54 in 100 in outpatient groups and 87 in 100 in inpatient groups; withdrawal at any time in life was reported much more often than in the past year. Reviews say it usually starts 1 to 2 days after stopping, is worst in the first week and fades within 1 to 2 weeks, and that it carries no serious medical risk for people without other illnesses. The studies defined regular use and withdrawal in different ways, and none checked how often the same feelings occur in people who do not cut down.
population: People with regular cannabis use or a cannabis use disorder in 50 observational cohorts (15 general-population, 28 outpatient, 7 inpatient or residential; 38 from North America), and people seeking help to stop, as described in narrative reviews
exposure: Stopping or cutting down after regular use (regular use as each cohort defined it; the review gives no common definition)
comparator: None (prevalence without a comparison group); settings and timeframes compared with each other
outcome: Cannabis withdrawal syndrome as each study defined it (DSM-5 in 5 cohorts, mostly earlier research definitions), at any time in life or in the past year; symptoms and time course as described in reviews
magnitude: Bahji 2020, random-effects pooled prevalence: general population 17% (95% CI 13 to 22; 15 cohorts; 17,475 people; I2 98%); outpatient 54% (48 to 59; 28; 5,684); inpatient 87% (79 to 94; 7; 357); past year 31% (27 to 36; 32 cohorts); lifetime 76% (70 to 82; 18); overall 47% (41 to 52; 50 cohorts; I2 99.2%; range 8% to 100%); men 27% (21 to 34), women 26% (19 to 33), P = .99; one DSM-5 population cohort 12.1% of 1,527. Editors' calculation on the card: 6,470 of 23,518 participants (27.5%). Time course as described in reviews: onset 1-2 days (24-48 hours), peak within the first week (2-6 days), resolution within 1-2 weeks.

risk_of_bias.note: Cohorts mostly rated fair (36 of 50) or poor (12) on the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale; clinical and residential samples selected for heavy use; lifetime withdrawal recalled in surveys; the lowest available threshold used; no comparison group to subtract background symptoms; the review is AMSTAR 2 critically low (card sc_bahji_2020).

inconsistency.note: I2 99.2% overall and 98% within general-population samples, whose estimates run from 7.6% to 34.4%; two analyses of one national survey gave 8.0% and 34.4%. Setting and timeframe explain part of the spread, not all.

indirectness.note: Regular use undefined; most definitions predate DSM-5; the pools include a prison survey and a synthetic-cannabinoid detoxification sample; the symptom description and time course are second-hand (narrative reviews).

imprecision.note: The setting estimates have intervals a few points wide.

publication_bias.note: Tests reported as negative (supplement not read); of little meaning for prevalence estimates.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (prevalence in the populations sampled): starts low; down one level each for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness: very low. The headline 47% is not used as the answer, because it averages cohorts of very different kinds and tracks the average cohort rather than the average participant (card sc_bahji_2020); the setting-specific figures are. The narrative reviews describe symptoms and time course second-hand and overlap with the meta-analysis (Connor et al., 2021, take their 54% and 87% from it), so they are not counted as further studies. Status replicated: in 50 cohorts from many teams withdrawal was found in some people who used regularly, consistently more often in clinical samples; how often varies widely, which the inconsistency rating carries.
